title: MasterFabric · Realtime Telco
tagline: Streaming network monitoring for a mobile operator, small enough to run on one laptop.
summary: This repository simulates a radio network of 240 cells sending 10-second KPI reports into Kafka the way real mediation chains deliver them: late, out of order and sometimes duplicated. Spark Structured Streaming turns the stream into Iceberg bronze, silver and gold tables, and a per-cell stateful detector built on EWMA z-scores, hard rules and a Bernoulli CUSUM raises typed alerts for outage, sleeping cell, congestion, interference and slow degradation, each scored against the ground truth that generated the telemetry. A later addition puts Apicurio schema registry and Flink 2.2 alongside the original Spark pipeline to measure Avro schema evolution, compare Flink against Spark on the same job, and test exactly-once delivery claims under kill -9. It is positioned as the streaming companion to the masterfabric-lakehouse-lab batch repository, with decisions recorded as ADRs.
keyResults: Live run: 240 cells over 6 simulated hours at 30x delivered 520,931 events in 12 minutes.
Detection on the held-out seed: 36/36 incidents found, 45 alerts, 2 false, precision 0.956, recall 1.0, type accuracy 1.0.
Static thresholds on the same windows: 334 alerts, 253 false, precision 0.243, 35/36 incidents found.
Latency from last report to alert: p50 9.8 s, p95 9.8 s (Kafka to watermark to silver to Iceberg stream to detector to MERGE and Kafka).
Data handling: 2,531 duplicates removed, 502 very late rows dropped by the watermark, 0 parse failures.
Throughput (drain): bronze 125,611 events/s, silver 74,689-94,561 events/s on Spark local[4] with 6 partitions.
Table maintenance: silver went from 357 files to 6 files, and a per-cell aggregate query improved from 736.9 ms to 43.5 ms.
Schema registry: BACKWARD rule accepted v2 and rejected incompatible v3 with HTTP 409; Avro records were 103 B versus 367 B for JSON.
Flink 2.2 vs Spark 3.5 on the same job: drain 3.07 s vs 10.54 s, live p50 2.6 s vs 4.1 s, CPU 12% vs 83%, with identical windows.
Exactly-once under kill -9: Flink's exactly-once sink had 0 duplicates versus 4,080 for at-least-once; Spark to Iceberg held all 521,044/521,044 offsets with 0 duplicates.

Watermark sweep (one recorded delivery, 173,701 deliveries of 172,800 reports, 2 simulated hours): reports lost were 2,999 at 10 s, 1,087 at 30 s, 190 at 1 min, 188 at the live 2 min, 178 at 5 min and 0 at 11 min; the window-end-to-emit delay at 2 min was 2.5 min versus 11.5 min at 11 min.

Late-data tests: seven watermark cases on the real silver code pass; with one watermark per query rather than per cell, a cell whose clock lags 3 minutes has every report after the first batch dropped.

Backpressure with silver alone capped at 1,000 records/s: latency p50 / max was 8.6 / 10.1 s at 0.5x input, 6.4 / 7.9 s at 1x, 18.4 / 31.6 s at 1.5x and 25.4 / 45.3 s at 1.9x; without the cap the same 1,935 events/s ran at p50 4.6 s, max 5.7 s.
limitations: Synthetic network: incidents are clean, labelled and single-cell, so the detector's measured precision and recall are an upper bound compared to real networks with correlated failures, maintenance windows and counter resets.

Alert flapping during long degradations: the 14 degradation incidents produced 23 alert openings because the capped CUSUM can dip under the threshold mid-incident and re-open; hysteresis is planned as the next change.
Simulated clock: event time runs 30x faster than wall time, so watermark waits and detection delays measured in wall-clock seconds are 30x shorter than they would be in production.
RocksDB memory grew to 94 MiB over the 12-minute live run while state rows stayed flat, and this was not investigated further.
Single broker, PLAINTEXT, local checkpoints: Kafka runs with replication factor 1 and no authentication; production would need RF 3, TLS/SASL and checkpoints on HDFS or S3.
Spark, not Flink, runs the main pipeline; the measured comparison shows Flink faster and much cheaper in CPU on the silver step, but the detector and Iceberg pipeline were not ported to Flink.
The engine comparison is limited to one laptop and one live run, with both engines sharing 6 vCPUs and nothing tuned (trigger, state backends, Kafka sink settings).
Late-data tests run on a file source, not Kafka: the sweep's emit delays are simulated time quantised by 30-second batches, and it covers one seed and one delivery profile (3% late, 0.1% very late).

Backpressure runs are short and single: one run per rate, one simulated hour each, silver query only, with Kafka and Spark sharing 6 vCPUs; the cap was set low on purpose, and consumer lag was not sampled directly.
Object storage is RustFS rather than MinIO, because MinIO images could not be pulled from the development machine.

images.alt: MasterFabric Realtime Telco: Kafka, Spark Structured Streaming, Iceberg and anomaly detection, with measured results

Kafka feeds two independent Spark queries (bronze, silver); the detector reads silver back as an Iceberg stream, so the contract between aggregation and detection is a table that any engine can query or replay.
One finalised minute for one cell passes through hard rules, adaptive z-scores and a Bernoulli CUSUM; the most severe condition wins, and the baseline learns only from calm windows.
Development seed only: false alerts against the median degradation delay for each CUSUM threshold; recall is 1.0 at every setting, and h = 14 was chosen.
Real silver windows from the live run around one incident of each kind; shaded is ground truth, red dashed is alert opened, green dashed is alert closed, and the flash crowd raised no alert.
The same 85,680 silver windows through the adaptive detector and a static rule set; static rules find almost as many incidents but bury them under 253 false alerts.
Wall-clock latency from the Kafka timestamp of a window's last report to the silver commit (85,680 windows) and to the alert (45 alerts).
Draining a pre-filled topic of 1,042,065 events with availableNow triggers; each configuration reads the whole topic, so bronze plus silver processes every event twice.
Live run micro-batches: batch durations stay under the 2-second trigger so no backlog builds, while silver state rows stay flat but RocksDB memory kept growing.
Spark UI during the live run: the three queries running side by side, about 724 input rows/s each for bronze and silver and 120 windows/s for the detector.
Silver query statistics: steady input rate, batch durations around 1 s, flat state rows, and a few rows per batch dropped by the watermark.
